transcript.heading: News Report One (American Female)
paras: The city of Boulder, Colorado, has launched an innovative community solar program that allows residents to subscribe to a shared solar farm and receive credits on their electricity bills, even if they cannot install solar panels on their own homes. The program, which is the largest of its kind in the state, includes a 20-acre solar array with over 20,000 panels capable of generating enough electricity to power approximately 1,200 homes annually. What makes this program unique is its focus on accessibility: low-income households can participate with no upfront costs and receive a 50 percent discount on their energy bills, while other residents pay a small subscription fee that still results in overall savings compared to standard electricity rates. City officials worked closely with local environmental groups and energy companies to develop the program, which was funded through a combination of government grants and private investment. Since subscriptions opened last month, over 700 households have already signed up, exceeding initial expectations. The city plans to expand the program with additional solar arrays over the next five years, with the goal of having 25 percent of the city's electricity come from community solar by 2031.

transcript.heading: News Report Two (British Male)
paras: The British Museum has announced a major new initiative to digitize its entire collection, making high-resolution images of more than 8 million objects available to the public for free online. The ambitious project, which is expected to take five years to complete, will allow anyone with internet access to view and study artifacts from the museum's vast collection, including ancient sculptures, paintings, coins, manuscripts, and archaeological finds from civilizations around the world. Museum officials say the digital archive will include detailed descriptions and historical context for each object, as well as 3D models for many items that users can rotate and examine from all angles. The museum has already begun the process with some of its most famous pieces, including the Rosetta Stone and the Parthenon Marbles, and aims to upload approximately 1.5 million objects per year until the collection is fully digitized. While the physical museum will remain open to visitors, curators hope that the digital collection will reach millions of people who may never have the opportunity to visit London in person, including students in developing countries and researchers who cannot travel to access the artifacts.

transcript.heading: News Report Three (American Male)
paras: Major online retailer Amazon has announced that it will begin using drones to deliver packages to customers in select cities within the next three months, marking a significant step forward for commercial drone delivery services. The company's new delivery drones, which have been in development for nearly a decade, are capable of carrying packages weighing up to five pounds and can fly at speeds of up to 50 miles per hour, enabling deliveries to be completed within 30 minutes of an order being placed. The drones use advanced GPS navigation and obstacle avoidance systems to safely navigate around buildings, trees, power lines, and other aircraft. Initially, the service will only be available in a few small to medium-sized cities, with eligible packages limited to small items such as books, electronics accessories, and household goods. Company executives say they have worked closely with aviation authorities to develop safety protocols and flight regulations, and that the drones will be monitored by human operators at all times during flights. While some privacy and safety advocates have raised concerns about drone noise and the potential for accidents, Amazon says extensive testing has shown the technology to be safe and reliable.

transcript.heading: Conversation One (British Female + British Male)
paras: Woman (Sarah): Hi, Tom. How's the graduation speech coming along? I can't believe commencement is only two weeks away! I'm getting really nervous just thinking about it.

Man (Tom): Oh hi, Sarah. It's coming along... slowly. I have a draft written, but I'm not sure if it's any good. I keep rewriting parts of it. What about you? You're the class valedictorian, so your speech is one of the main events! I'm just giving the student government farewell address, which is shorter.

Woman: I know, that's why I'm so stressed! I want it to be meaningful and memorable, but I don't want to bore everyone with clichés. Right now, I'm trying to decide what main theme to focus on. Do I talk about the future and our potential? Or do I look back at our shared memories over the past four years?

Man: Why not do a bit of both? People love hearing shared memories because they can relate to them—it makes them feel connected. But you also want to leave people feeling inspired and excited about what comes next. Maybe you could start with a funny story from freshman year to get people laughing and engaged, then transition into talking about how those experiences prepared us for the future.

Woman: That's a good idea! I was thinking about opening with the story of moving into the dorms and getting lost on the first day—remember how half of us ended up in the wrong buildings because the maps were confusing? That was pretty chaotic but also really funny when we look back on it.

Man: Oh, I definitely remember that! Everyone was helping each other find their rooms even though we were all lost too. That's actually a perfect example of how we supported each other through college, not just that day but throughout all four years—during midterms, when we were stressed about internships, all those late nights in the library.

Woman: Exactly! That sense of community is what I really want to emphasize. College wasn't just about getting a degree for me; it was about the people we met and the friendships we made. But I'm also worried about keeping the speech the right length. The dean told me I should speak for no more than eight minutes. I tend to ramble when I get nervous.

Man: Eight minutes is actually pretty short—maybe 1,000 to 1,200 words? You should time yourself practicing out loud, not just reading silently. When people are nervous, they tend to speak faster, but sometimes pauses for laughter or applause add time too. Also, remember to make eye contact with different parts of the audience instead of just reading straight from your notes. It makes the speech feel more personal.

Woman: That's really helpful advice. Are you going to practice your speech in front of anyone? I was thinking about asking my roommate to listen to me and give feedback. I'm also worried about tripping going up to the stage, or my microphone not working, or all sorts of silly things.

Man: I know what you mean—those little things can feel like huge disasters when you're already nervous. But just remember that everyone in the audience is on your side. They're all there to celebrate, and they'll be supportive even if something goes wrong. And honestly, most people probably won't even remember any small mistakes. They'll just remember how the speech made them feel.

Woman: You're right. I think I'm overthinking it. Let's make a deal—we'll both practice our speeches for each other this weekend, give honest feedback, and then go out for ice cream afterward to celebrate being almost done.
Man: That sounds like a perfect plan. Let's meet in the library study room on Saturday afternoon. We'll be graduation speech pros by the end of it!

transcript.heading: Conversation Two (American Female + American Male)
paras: Woman (Megan): Hey, Chris! How was your weekend? I saw you posted pictures from that new cooking school downtown. Did you take a class?

Man (Chris): Hey Megan! Yeah, I did a Thai cooking class on Saturday afternoon. It was so much fun, and the food we made was incredible. I've been wanting to learn how to cook proper Thai food for ages because I love ordering it at restaurants, but I could never get the flavors right when I tried at home.

Woman: That sounds amazing! I didn't know you were into cooking. I usually just make simple pasta dishes or order takeout because I never learned how to cook anything more complicated. What was the class like? Were there a lot of people?

Man: It was actually a small class, only about eight people, which was nice because the instructor could give everyone individual attention. We started by going over the essential ingredients in Thai cooking—things like lemongrass, galangal, fish sauce, kaffir lime leaves, and different types of curry paste. Then we each made three dishes: green curry with chicken, pad Thai, and mango sticky rice for dessert. The instructor walked us through each step, and we got to eat everything we made at the end.
Woman: That sounds like such a fun activity. Was it expensive? I've always thought cooking classes were kind of pricey.

Man: It was $75 per person for the three-hour class, which included all the ingredients, recipes to take home, and the meal at the end. I thought it was pretty reasonable, actually, especially since we got to learn proper techniques from a professional chef. They offer a bunch of different classes—Italian, French, Japanese, Indian, even baking workshops. I'm thinking about taking the sushi-making class next month.

Woman: I've always wanted to learn how to make sushi, but I'm intimidated by the rice. It seems like it has to be just the right consistency. Do you think they offer classes for absolute beginners? I can barely boil an egg without burning it.

Man: Definitely! The class I took was designed for beginners, and the chef was really patient with everyone, even the people who had trouble chopping vegetables properly. She explained everything really clearly, from basic knife skills to how to balance the sweet, sour, salty, and spicy flavors that are so important in Thai cooking. You should come with me to the sushi class! It would be fun to go together.

Woman: That's really tempting! But I'm worried I'd be terrible at it and make a fool of myself. Also, do you get to take home anything besides the recipes? Like, do you get to keep the tools or anything?

Man: You don't keep the tools, but they provide everything you need during class. And honestly, everyone was too focused on their own cooking to pay attention to anyone else's mistakes. The instructor said that making mistakes is actually how you learn to cook better. If a dish didn't turn out perfectly, she would help us fix it and explain what went wrong.

Woman: Okay, you've convinced me! Let me know when you sign up for the sushi class, and I'll join you. Maybe after a few classes, I'll actually be able to cook dinner for my friends instead of always ordering pizza.
Man: That's the spirit! And if nothing else, we get to eat a delicious meal at the end. I'll send you the link to their schedule tonight, and we can pick a date that works for both of us.

transcript.heading: Passage One (British Male)
paras: The development of efficient public transportation systems is essential for the sustainable growth of modern cities, yet many urban areas continue to struggle with traffic congestion, air pollution, and inadequate transit options. Cities around the world are pursuing different strategies to improve public transit and reduce reliance on private automobiles.

One approach that has been successful in many European and Asian cities is investing in high-quality rail systems, including subways, light rail, and commuter trains. Cities like Tokyo, Paris, and Singapore have extensive subway networks that are fast, reliable, and affordable, making it possible for millions of people to commute daily without cars. These systems are particularly effective because they operate on dedicated tracks, avoiding the traffic congestion that slows down buses on roads. However, building subway systems is extremely expensive, often costing billions of dollars, which makes it difficult for many cities to afford.

Bus rapid transit, or BRT, systems offer a more affordable alternative to rail. BRT systems use dedicated bus lanes, off-board fare collection, and specially designed stations to provide bus service that is almost as fast and reliable as rail transit but at a fraction of the cost. Cities like Curitiba in Brazil and Bogotá in Colombia have become famous for their successful BRT systems, which have significantly reduced travel times and increased public transit usage. Many other cities, particularly in developing countries, have adopted the BRT model as a cost-effective way to improve public transportation.

Technology is also playing an increasingly important role in improving public transit. Many cities now use real-time tracking apps that allow passengers to see exactly when their bus or train will arrive, reducing waiting times and making transit more predictable. Contactless payment systems make boarding faster and more convenient, while data analytics help transit agencies optimize routes and schedules based on actual usage patterns. Some cities are also experimenting with on-demand microtransit services—small buses or vans that passengers can book through a smartphone app to pick them up and drop them off close to their destinations, providing a more flexible alternative to fixed-route bus services.

transcript.heading: Passage Two (American Female)
paras: Volunteer travel, also known as voluntourism, has become an increasingly popular way for people to combine travel with meaningful work that benefits local communities and conservation efforts. Unlike traditional vacations where the primary focus is relaxation or sightseeing, volunteer trips allow participants to contribute their time and skills to projects around the world, from teaching English in rural schools and building homes for low-income families to participating in wildlife conservation and environmental restoration.

There are many potential benefits to volunteer travel. For participants, it offers an opportunity to immerse themselves in a different culture in a way that typical tourism does not—volunteers often live with local families or in community housing, eat local food, and develop deeper connections with the places they visit. Many volunteers report that the experience is personally transformative, helping them develop new skills, gain perspective on global issues, and build confidence. For local communities, well-organized volunteer projects can provide much-needed labor and resources, as well as cultural exchange and skills transfer. Projects like building schools or providing medical care can have lasting positive impacts when done in partnership with local organizations.

However, volunteer travel also has its critics, who point out that poorly planned voluntourism can do more harm than good. One major concern is the phenomenon of "orphanage tourism," where well-meaning volunteers pay to work in children's homes, inadvertently creating financial incentives for institutions that may separate children from their families or prioritize profit over child welfare. Short-term volunteers who lack appropriate qualifications may also disrupt local services—for example, unskilled volunteers attempting to do construction work may create safety hazards, while those without teaching training may do little to improve educational outcomes. There are also environmental concerns, as long-distance travel to volunteer destinations contributes to carbon emissions, and some conservation projects may prioritize tourist experiences over actual environmental protection.

Experts recommend that anyone considering volunteer travel thoroughly research organizations before signing up, looking for programs that prioritize long-term community development, work closely with local partners, and match volunteers' skills to actual needs. The most effective volunteer experiences tend to be those where volunteers commit to longer stays, have relevant skills to offer, and approach the experience with humility and a willingness to learn from local communities rather than assuming they have all the answers.

transcript.heading: Passage Three (American Male)
paras: Students have long been told that getting a good night's sleep is important before an exam, but recent scientific research has revealed just how critical sleep is for memory and learning, with implications for how students should structure their study schedules.

Scientists have discovered that sleep plays a crucial role in memory consolidation—the process by which newly learned information is transferred from short-term memory to more permanent long-term storage. This process appears to occur primarily during deep slow-wave sleep, which typically happens in the early part of the night, and during rapid eye movement, or REM, sleep, which is more common later in the sleep cycle. During these sleep stages, the brain appears to replay and reorganize information learned during the day, strengthening important neural connections and integrating new knowledge with existing memories.

Research has demonstrated that sleep benefits different types of learning in different ways. For declarative memory—facts and information that you can consciously recall, like vocabulary words or historical dates—sleep before learning helps prepare the brain to encode new information effectively. Studies show that people who sleep before memorizing new material retain significantly more than those who are sleep-deprived. Sleep after learning is equally important, as it helps cement the new memories and protects them from being forgotten. Even a short nap of 60 to 90 minutes, which can include both slow-wave and REM sleep, has been shown to improve memory retention compared to staying awake for the same period.

Perhaps surprisingly, sleep also enhances procedural memory—the type of memory involved in learning skills and motor tasks, like playing a musical instrument, typing, or solving certain types of mathematical problems. Research shows that performance on skill-based tasks can actually improve after sleep without additional practice, as the brain continues to process and refine the learned skills during rest. This means that practicing a skill in the evening and then "sleeping on it" can lead to better performance the next day.

These findings have important implications for study habits. Pulling all-nighters to cram for exams, a common practice among college students, is actually counterproductive because it deprives the brain of the sleep it needs to consolidate what has been learned. Students who stay up all night studying may remember information for a few hours during the exam, but they will retain much less long-term compared to those who study and then get a full night's sleep. Research suggests that the most effective study strategy is to spread studying out over multiple days (a technique known as spaced repetition) rather than cramming, and to prioritize getting adequate sleep, especially the night after learning new material and the night before an exam. Even a short nap after studying can provide significant memory benefits if a full night's sleep isn't possible.
